# Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents

Ruhan Wang    Yucheng Shi    Zongxia Li    Junyao Yang    Zhongzhi Li   
Yue Yu    Haitao Mi    Dongruo Zhou    Leoweiliang Affiliation: \[
Affiliation: \[ Affiliation: \[ Affiliation: \[ Affiliation: \[

October 19, 2026

###### Abstract

Long-horizon terminal agents may complete a task in one run yet fail to
do so consistently across repeated runs. Stochastic generation can
introduce local errors that propagate through subsequent actions and
context, creating a gap between task-solving ability and reliable
execution. The harness controls command execution, feedback, context
management, and completion decisions, providing a direct way to address
this gap. The effectiveness of these mechanisms depends on the model’s
behavior. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving
agent harnesses while keeping model weights fixed. RiseHarness focuses
on _flipping tasks_, which have both successful and failed runs under
the same configuration. Successful runs establish that the current
system can complete the task and provide references for analyzing
failures. The analysis combines agent trajectories with internal harness
traces collected by a runtime monitor, examining both the model’s
actions and how the harness executes them, presents feedback, and
controls the interaction. A Harness Handbook connects this evidence to
specific harness behaviors and their source code, helping identify
recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. To address these
problems, RiseHarness searches other harness frameworks for relevant
implementations and uses them as design references, taking into account
the current execution flow, interaction protocol, available signals, and
model behavior. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated
task evaluation; versions with measured gains become the basis for the
next iteration. This loop progressively integrates suitable mechanisms
from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution
evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and
reliability across models, use ablations to examine the contributions of
harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to
unseen benchmarks with the same model. The framework treats a specific
model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared
interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable
across tasks.

## 1 Introduction

A model that solves a long-horizon terminal task once may fail to do so
consistently. Across many interactions, an incorrect command or a missed
observation can change the environment and the context available for
later decisions. Stochastic generation can therefore lead to different
outcomes even when the task and model remain unchanged. Long-horizon
terminal benchmarks examine workflows requiring hundreds of interactions
and sustained progress \[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2)\]. This
distinction between reaching a successful outcome and succeeding
reliably across repeated runs is central to agent evaluation
\[[3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4)\]. We study how to narrow this gap by
improving the harness around a fixed model.

Training-based approaches improve terminal agents through reinforcement
learning and verified task synthesis \[[5](#bib.bib5), [6](#bib.bib6)\].
The harness controls command execution, observation feedback, context
management, and completion decisions. Interface design can affect agent
performance without updating model weights \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], and the
harness itself has become a target for automatic improvement. Execution
traces and evaluation feedback can guide changes to harness code and
support the evaluation of their effects \[[8](#bib.bib8),
[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)\]. Failure-informed runtime
interventions have also been studied as a way to improve repeated
success without changing model weights \[[11](#bib.bib11)\].

Our focus is how to connect differences between successful and failed
runs to actual internal harness behavior, identify shared mechanisms to
improve, and use implementations from other frameworks as references for
changes suited to the current harness and model. A difference between
two trajectories does not by itself establish that a harness behavior is
missing: the harness may already provide the relevant feedback, or the
information needed for a proposed intervention may not be available.
Likewise, an effective design in another framework may depend on
different interfaces or execution conditions. We introduce RiseHarness,
which uses execution evidence to check these conditions and to design
and validate changes. With the evaluated model held fixed, its evolution
loop combines comparisons of successful and failed runs, internal
execution analysis, and research into existing implementations.

We begin with _flipping tasks_, which have both successful and failed
runs under the same model and harness configuration. Successful runs
show that the current system can solve the task and provide references
for analyzing failures. Same-task trajectory contrast and cross-task
aggregation help identify recurring behavioral problems
\[[12](#bib.bib12)\]. In RiseHarness, the contrast first identifies a
behavioral need; the analysis then checks whether the current harness
can support that behavior and whether it already performs it. A runtime
monitor records internal execution and aligns these harness traces with
agent trajectories, exposing how proposed actions are dispatched and how
feedback reaches the model. We use the Harness Handbook
\[[13](#bib.bib13)\] to connect these records to behavioral
responsibilities and implementing code. This joint analysis helps
distinguish an agent’s unsuccessful response from a missing or
ineffective harness mechanism and groups supported findings into targets
for shared changes.

External documentation can inform the implementation of agent
capabilities \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. RiseHarness searches other
frameworks, source code, and technical documentation for implementations
relevant to the behavioral problems identified through execution
analysis. For completion decisions, for example, it can examine how
other frameworks track unfinished commands or verify results. The system
studies the signals and interfaces these designs require, then considers
the current harness’s execution flow, available information, and model
behavior to decide which ideas are applicable and how to modify existing
mechanisms. The goal is to draw on useful designs from different
frameworks to develop a harness whose mechanisms work together for the
current model.

Behavioral checks assess whether a candidate implements the intended
change, while repeated task evaluations measure its effect on
performance. Accepted changes provide the basis for subsequent rounds;
unsuccessful candidates supply execution evidence for revising the
implementation or proposed mechanism. Model weights remain fixed
throughout.

RiseHarness evolves the harness for a specific model based on its
execution behavior. Models may require different forms of interaction
support \[[15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16)\]; we therefore conduct
evolution separately for each model and examine the resulting behavioral
changes. These changes affect shared mechanisms for command execution,
observation feedback, and completion. Their benefits beyond the
evolution tasks require separate validation. Repeated evaluations and
ablations assess the effects on task success and execution reliability,
as well as the contributions of dual-trace evidence and research into
external implementations. We then hold both the model and the evolved
harness fixed and evaluate on benchmarks not used for evolution to test
whether these behavioral improvements support a broader range of tasks.

Our main contributions are:

- •
  An evidence-driven harness evolution framework. We introduce
  RiseHarness, which uses successful runs as references for failed runs
  and iteratively retains harness changes that improve measured
  performance without updating model weights.
- •
  Behavioral diagnosis from paired runs and internal execution. We
  combine agent and harness traces with the Harness Handbook to check
  proposed behavioral needs against actual execution and locate shared
  mechanisms for modification.
- •
  Harness modification informed by external implementations. We retrieve
  relevant implementations from other frameworks, examine their
  requirements, and use the current harness’s structure, runtime
  signals, and model behavior to design specific changes.
- •
  Reliability and generalization. Repeated runs and ablations assess
  harness evidence and external research; we compare changes across
  models and test cross-benchmark transfer with the model held fixed.

## 2 Related Work

##### Long-horizon execution and success consistency.

Long-horizon agents must coordinate reasoning, actions, and execution
feedback across many interactions \[[17](#bib.bib17),
[18](#bib.bib18)\]. Long-Horizon-Terminal-Bench and its 2.0 extension
use intermediate grading to measure progress through extended workflows
\[[1](#bib.bib1), [2](#bib.bib2)\]. Local errors can alter the
environment and subsequent context, leading to different outcomes for
the same model and task. Average success alone therefore does not fully
capture execution reliability. $`\tau`$-bench measures consistency
through $`\mathrm{pass}^{k}`$, the proportion of tasks solved in all
$`k`$ repeated trials \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]; broader reliability research
also examines robustness, predictability, and safety \[[4](#bib.bib4)\].
AgentDebug diagnoses errors and supplies corrective feedback for
recovery \[[19](#bib.bib19)\]; AgentRx localizes failures using
constraints and evidence-bearing validation logs \[[20](#bib.bib20)\].
FIRE studies failure-informed runtime interventions that improve
repeated success without updating model weights \[[11](#bib.bib11)\].
These studies motivate examining whether an agent system can
consistently support successful execution, beyond whether its model can
solve a task at all. We study tasks with both successful and failed runs
to assess whether harness changes can narrow this gap.

##### Agent harnesses.

The harness is the runtime layer that organizes model–environment
interaction, including command execution, observation construction,
context management, and completion decisions. SWE-agent shows that
interface design affects task performance with a fixed model
\[[7](#bib.bib7)\]. OpenHands provides composable tools, memory
management, sandboxed execution, and lifecycle control, illustrating the
components of this layer \[[21](#bib.bib21)\]. Memory, planning, and
action modules also appear in agentic recommender architectures
\[[22](#bib.bib22)\]. Understanding how a harness affects execution
requires both runtime observations and knowledge of its implementation.
AgentTrace records runtime activity and model interactions
\[[23](#bib.bib23)\], while the Harness Handbook links behavioral
responsibilities to implementing code, providing a behavior-oriented
basis for analysis and modification \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. HarnessBank
and HarnessDev further show that the effects of harness changes can
depend on the runtime model \[[15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16)\].
Harness design thus requires understanding both its internal mechanisms
and how the model responds to them.

Algorithm 1 RiseHarness: harness self-evolution

##### Harness self-evolution.

Automated agent design optimizes prompts, workflows, and executable
agents \[[24](#bib.bib24), [25](#bib.bib25), [26](#bib.bib26),
[27](#bib.bib27), [28](#bib.bib28)\]. Iterative response refinement is
also studied in federated in-context learning and uncertainty-aware
reasoning \[[29](#bib.bib29), [30](#bib.bib30)\]. Verified trajectory
rewriting and recursive policy refinement improve terminal models
through training \[[31](#bib.bib31), [32](#bib.bib32)\]. AHE,
HarnessFix, and Meta-Harness use execution evidence and evaluation
feedback to guide harness updates \[[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10),
[8](#bib.bib8)\]. ModularRSI contrasts successful and failed runs,
aggregates findings across tasks, and evolves modular components
\[[12](#bib.bib12)\]. Self-Harness analyzes failures and retains
fixed-model edits through regression tests \[[33](#bib.bib33)\].
HarnessEvolve also uses successful references for failure analysis, but
generates and verifies them with access to ground-truth answers
\[[34](#bib.bib34)\]. Related work explores design reuse
\[[35](#bib.bib35)\], external documentation \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], and
controls against benchmark overfitting \[[36](#bib.bib36)\]. Evaluation
studies also emphasize matched-budget search baselines and held-out
tests \[[37](#bib.bib37)\]. Our framework combines same-configuration
successes, dual traces, and the Handbook to check behavioral needs, then
consults external implementations to design local changes. Candidates
undergo implementation checks and repeated evaluation; transfer is
assessed separately with the harness held fixed.

## 3 Harness Self-Evolution

RiseHarness is a harness self-evolution framework for long-horizon
agents. It uses execution evidence and external design knowledge to
iteratively improve execution reliability while keeping model weights
fixed. We first introduce the basic concepts and notation in the
preliminaries. We then describe the four components of the
method—execution recording and behavior localization, problem discovery
and grouping, mechanism research and adaptation, and implementation and
validation—with reference to Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

### 3.1 Preliminaries

Let $`M_{\theta}`$ denote the evaluated model and $`\mathcal{D}`$ the
development task set. Both remain fixed throughout evolution, as do the
task protocol, verifier, and acceptance rules. Modifications are
confined to harness prompts and executable interaction logic; the model
proposing them may differ from $`M_{\theta}`$. At round $`t`$, the
current harness $`H_{t}`$ has a corresponding Handbook $`K_{t}`$ and a
reference corpus $`R_{t}`$ containing outcomes and dual traces from
$`r_{t}\geq 2`$ complete repetitions per task. The initial corpus
$`R_{0}`$ is collected by repeatedly running the seed harness $`H_{0}`$
on $`\mathcal{D}`$.

The basic analysis unit is a pair $`p`$ of successful and failed runs of
the same task under the same model and harness configuration. The paired
agent and harness traces are denoted by $`p^{a}`$ and $`p^{h}`$,
respectively. A _wish_ specifies the behavior expected from the harness
under an observable condition. A _finding_ consists of a revised wish,
assessments of whether the required information was available and the
behavior had already been performed, and supporting execution evidence.
The finding set $`\mathcal{A}`$ is partitioned into behavioral groups
$`\mathcal{G}`$: findings in one group could be addressed by a shared
harness change. Each finding belongs to one group, while a single run
pair may yield several findings assigned to different groups. The
selected groups are denoted by $`\mathcal{G}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{G}`$.

Let $`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ denote the proposals for round $`t`$, $`C_{t}`$
an implemented candidate harness, and $`K_{t}^{C}`$ its updated
Handbook. The candidate’s full evaluation outcomes and traces are
denoted by $`E_{t}`$. The history $`\mathcal{L}`$ records proposals,
results, and feedback across rounds; the policy $`\Pi`$ specifies
checking, screening, baseline, and stopping rules. The aggregate pass
rate of the candidate is denoted by $`\widehat{p}(E_{t})`$, and
$`\widehat{p}_{B}^{\,\mathrm{confirm}}(\mathcal{D})`$ denotes the
confirmation baseline specified by $`\Pi`$. These quantities determine
whether a candidate is adopted, as detailed in Section
[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Validation and Evolution ‣ 3 Harness Self-Evolution ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

### 3.2 Execution Evidence

Improving a harness first requires distinguishing the model’s requested
actions from the system’s actual behavior. An agent trajectory
$`\tau^{\mathrm{agent}}`$ records the information the model receives,
its responses, and tool interactions, but does not fully expose internal
harness processing. A requested command, for example, may not be
dispatched, and terminal output may not be returned to the model in
full. The agent trajectory alone may therefore be insufficient to locate
the problem.

RiseHarness uses a runtime monitor to record calling relationships,
arguments, return values, exceptions, and source locations at selected
harness function boundaries, producing a harness trace
$`\tau^{\mathrm{harness}}`$. Run identifiers and episode indices link
the two traces, allowing the analysis to follow a model request through
its processing and the feedback ultimately returned. Both traces,
together with task outcomes and execution identities, are retained in
the reference corpus $`R_{t}`$.

Function-level records must also be connected to behavior. Because a
single harness behavior may span several functions, RiseHarness uses a
Handbook $`K_{t}`$ aligned with the current source to describe
behavioral responsibilities, triggers, implementing functions, and exit
conditions \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. These mappings connect individual calls
to command execution, observation handling, context management, and
completion checks. They explain each call’s role in the overall
mechanism and help locate the relevant code.

The traces thus establish what happened, while the Handbook identifies
the behavior involved and its implementation. For a pair $`p`$, the
paired agent and harness traces $`p^{a}`$ and $`p^{h}`$ provide
execution evidence. The Handbook $`K_{t}`$ connects these records to
harness behavior during analysis (line
[8](#alg1.l8 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"))
and supports mechanism adaptation during proposal generation (line
[9](#alg1.l9 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).
Initial seed runs supply $`R_{0}`$; candidate screening and full
evaluation use the same recording process (lines
[14](#alg1.l14 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")–[15](#alg1.l15 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")),
supplying new execution evidence for subsequent iterations.

### 3.3 Behavioral Analysis

This stage identifies behavioral problems in repeated runs and groups
related findings into targets for harness improvement. We focus on
flipping tasks, which have both successful and failed runs under the
same model and harness configuration. Successful runs show that the
current system can complete the task and provide concrete references for
examining failures. Let $`y_{i,j}(H_{t})\in\{0,1\}`$ indicate whether
task $`i`$ succeeds in repetition $`j`$ under harness $`H_{t}`$. The
flipping task set in $`R_{t}`$ is

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{F}_{t}=\left\{i:\ 0<\sum_{j=1}^{r_{t}}y_{i,j}(H_{t})<r_{t}\right\}.
``` |  | (1) |

For each flipping task, the system pairs successful and failed runs,
examines relevant interactions, and uses their execution differences to
formulate behavioral wishes. Each wish is checked against the
information available to the harness and the mechanisms it actually
executed at the time. Findings from individual pairs are then pooled to
identify shared behavioral needs across tasks. Four operations implement
this process (Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"),
lines
[8](#alg1.l8 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")–[9](#alg1.l9 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")):

|  Operation |  Role |
|----|----|
|  $`{\color[rgb]{0.207,0.3984,0.6523}\mathop{\text{Compare}}\nolimits}`$ |  Compare relevant interactions, identify execution differences, and use the Handbook to interpret the harness’s role. |
|  $`{\color[rgb]{0.5898,0.3945,0.1133}\mathop{\text{Wish}}\nolimits}`$ |  Use comparison evidence and agent traces to specify what the harness should do and under which observable conditions. |
|  $`{\color[rgb]{0.1484,0.4648,0.4258}\mathop{\text{Revise}}\nolimits}`$ |  Inspect harness traces to assess whether the required information was available and the existing mechanism had already performed the behavior; revise the wish accordingly. |
|  $`{\color[rgb]{0.4609,0.3281,0.6094}\mathop{\text{Group}}\nolimits}`$ |  Pool findings across pairs, group those that could be addressed by a shared behavioral change, and formulate a common wish. |

The first three operations produce the finding set $`\mathcal{A}`$,
retaining revised wishes, assessments, and supporting evidence. A single
run pair may expose several problems and therefore yield findings
assigned to different groups.

After grouping, an independent review checks whether each common wish
applies to all members and whether the groups correspond to distinct
modification needs. Review feedback guides regrouping. Groups that
remain disputed or are excluded by the history $`\mathcal{L}`$ do not
proceed to proposal generation. The remaining groups are ranked by
distinct-task coverage, distinct failing runs, and finding count to
select $`\mathcal{G}_{t}`$. Each selected group carries its common wish
and complete member evidence into the next stage of mechanism research
and design.

### 3.4 Design Exploration

This stage turns shared behavioral wishes into concrete harness
modification proposals. Given the selected groups $`\mathcal{G}_{t}`$,
current harness $`H_{t}`$, Handbook $`K_{t}`$, and reference corpus
$`R_{t}`$, $`\mathop{\text{Propose}}\nolimits`$ examines implementations
in other frameworks to generate proposals $`\mathcal{P}_{t}`$ (line
[9](#alg1.l9 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).

The system first uses group evidence, the Handbook, and source code to
identify the behavior to improve, its current implementation, and the
available runtime information. It then translates the common wish into
search questions. The search examines how other harnesses handle similar
problems, including their execution flow, maintained state, and feedback
to the model. For information loss in long command outputs, for example,
it can investigate how full outputs are saved, key information is
presented, and later retrieval is supported. Retrieved implementations
and their sources are retained as references for designing local
changes.

The system then designs changes suited to the current harness’s
structure, interaction protocol, and model behavior observed in the
traces. Each design specifies how the borrowed ideas would affect
existing mechanisms, where the required information would come from, and
whether additional state or interface support is needed. The system also
examines traces from tasks that succeeded in every recorded repetition
to assess whether the proposed intervention could disrupt successful
execution and to refine its triggers and scope.

The resulting proposals specify behavioral changes, implementation
sites, dependencies, and additional interaction costs, along with
expected outcomes and observations for testing them. Each proposal links
its execution evidence and external design sources for subsequent
implementation and validation. If no suitable external precedent is
found, the system retains the search record and may propose an
explicitly identified local design.

### 3.5 Validation and Evolution

Once proposals are generated, $`\mathop{\text{Implement}}\nolimits`$
applies them to the current harness $`H_{t}`$ to build a candidate
$`C_{t}`$, together with its updated Handbook $`K_{t}^{C}`$ and trace
recording configuration (Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"),
line
[13](#alg1.l13 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).
The system checks that the candidate can run and record traces. When
enabled, independent behavioral checks (Appendix
[A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 Behavioral Validation ‣ Appendix A System Implementation ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"))
test whether each change produces the expected behavior under the
specified conditions. Problems found during checking are fed back for
repair within a predefined attempt limit. Only candidates that pass
these checks proceed to task evaluation.

Evaluation proceeds through screening followed by full validation.
$`\mathop{\text{Screen}}\nolimits`$ examines task outcomes and mechanism
activation on proposal-related tasks to select a configuration for
validation. $`\mathop{\text{Evaluate}}\nolimits`$ then collects fresh
repeated runs on the development set $`\mathcal{D}`$, producing outcomes
and dual traces $`E_{t}`$ (lines
[14](#alg1.l14 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")–[15](#alg1.l15 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).
Adoption depends on this full evaluation: the records must be valid, the
required run set complete, and the aggregate pass rate higher than the
declared comparison baseline (line
[17](#alg1.l17 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).

On adoption, $`\mathop{\text{Publish}}\nolimits`$ saves the candidate
and its Handbook as $`H_{t+1}`$ and $`K_{t+1}`$, and uses $`E_{t}`$ as
the next reference corpus $`R_{t+1}`$ (line
[18](#alg1.l18 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).
Source code, mechanism settings, and recording configuration are saved
with the version, keeping the implementation, behavioral description,
and execution evidence aligned for the next round. If the candidate is
not adopted, the current version and its reference data are retained.

Checking and evaluation records from each round are added to the history
$`\mathcal{L}`$ to guide subsequent search (line
[20](#alg1.l20 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).
Based on this evidence, the system decides whether to repair the
implementation, revise proposal requirements, or try other proposals.
$`\mathop{\text{Revisit}}\nolimits`$ returns existing proposals to the
same implementation and validation process (line
[11](#alg1.l11 "In Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).
After a new version is adopted, discovery resumes with the updated
execution evidence. Iteration ends at the round limit or another
configured stopping condition.

## 4 Experiments

We evaluate RiseHarness across models to examine its effects on task
success and execution reliability in long-horizon terminal tasks. We use
ablations to assess the contributions of key components and evaluate
evolved harnesses on benchmarks not used for evolution to examine
transfer. Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1 "Models and benchmarks. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
describes the models, benchmarks, baselines, and evaluation protocol.
The remaining subsections address the following four research questions:

- •
  RQ1: Compared with the seed harness and existing baselines, can
  RiseHarness improve task success and repeated-run reliability across
  models? (Section
  [4.2](#S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1 "Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"))
- •
  RQ2: How does removing harness traces and the Handbook, or omitting
  external design research, affect harness evolution? (Section
  [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Component Contributions ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"))
- •
  RQ3: How do retained harness changes vary across models in their
  behavioral targets and intervention mechanisms? (Section
  [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Adaptation and Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"))
- •
  RQ4: With the model and evolved harness fixed, do gains in task
  success and reliability transfer to benchmarks not used for evolution?
  (Section
  [4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Adaptation and Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"))

### 4.1 Experimental Setup

##### Models and benchmarks.

We evaluate RiseHarness on GPT-6-sol and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, keeping
model weights fixed throughout harness evolution. For each model, we
start from the unmodified Terminus-2 harness and evolve it on
Terminal-Bench Hard (TBH), a benchmark of 100 challenging terminal tasks
described by [Li et al. \[31\]](#bib.bib31). Repeated runs on TBH
provide both execution trajectories for behavioral analysis and task
outcomes for evaluating changes and selecting harness versions. To
assess cross-benchmark generalization, we freeze the evolved harnesses
and test them on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (TB2.1), which contains 89 tasks
\[[38](#bib.bib38)\]. TB2.1 is used only for transfer evaluation and
does not inform harness modifications.

##### Baselines and evaluation protocol.

We compare RiseHarness with the seed Terminus-2 harness, ModularRSI
\[[12](#bib.bib12)\], and AHE Harness \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. We also
include two ablation baselines to assess the contributions of key
components:

- •
  RiseHarness w/o Harness Evidence: analysis uses only agent traces and
  source code, without harness traces or the Harness Handbook.
- •
  RiseHarness w/o External Research: analysis retains dual traces and
  the Handbook, but proposals are generated from local information
  without external research.

Full RiseHarness and both ablation baselines start from the same seed
harness and reference runs, with matched models, editable scope, and
predefined budgets. Apart from the removed components, their procedures
are identical (Section
[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Component Contributions ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).
We evaluate the publicly released ModularRSI harness without
re-evolution. Each selected harness is frozen before independent
repeated evaluation. The reference-baseline and version-selection rules
used during evolution are specified in Appendices
[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Comparison Protocol ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Methodology ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and
[C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Result Reporting ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Methodology ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

##### Metrics and reporting.

We measure both average task performance and repeated-run reliability.
Unless otherwise stated, each task is evaluated in $`r=4`$ repeated
runs. For task $`i`$ and repetition $`j`$, let $`y_{i,j}(H)=1`$ denote a
pass under harness $`H`$ and $`y_{i,j}(H)=0`$ a scored failure. Scoring
and completeness rules are specified in Appendix
[C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Repeated Evaluation ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Methodology ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

For a task set $`S`$, we report four metrics, distinguishing average
success from reliability across repeated runs \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]:

- •
  Pass@1: the average pass rate over all tasks and repetitions,
  measuring performance in a single run.
- •
  Pass^(r): the fraction of tasks that pass in all $`r`$ runs, measuring
  repeated-run success reliability.
- •
  Pass@$`r`$: the fraction of tasks that pass at least once in $`r`$
  runs, measuring observed task coverage within a limited number of
  attempts.
- •
  Flip: the fraction of tasks with both successful and failed runs,
  measuring outcome inconsistency.

On a complete trial grid, let $`N=|S|`$ and
$`k_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}y_{i,j}(H)`$ be the number of successful runs for
task $`i`$. Suppressing the common harness argument, the metrics are

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Pass@1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Nr}\sum_{i\in S}k_{i},`$ | $`\displaystyle\qquad\mathrm{Pass}^{r}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in S}\mathbb{I}[k_{i}=r],`$ |  | (2) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{Pass@}r`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i\in S}\mathbb{I}[k_{i}>0],`$ | $`\displaystyle\qquad\mathrm{Flip}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathrm{Pass@}r-\mathrm{Pass}^{r}.`$ |  |  |

Changes denote absolute differences between the reported rates. Pass@1
corresponds to the aggregate pass rate $`\widehat{p}(H;S,r)`$ used for
version selection. A lower Flip alone does not imply more reliable
success: a flipping task may instead become an all-failure task. We
therefore interpret Flip together with Pass^(r). Aggregate category
changes do not establish which initially stable tasks have regressed;
that requires per-task comparisons. During evolution, aggregate pass
rate determines whether a change is adopted; reliability is reported
separately.

### 4.2 Performance and Reliability

##### Overall performance.

Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
summarizes task performance for RiseHarness and the comparison
baselines. Relative to the seed Terminus-2 harness, RiseHarness improves
both average success and repeated-run reliability across the two models,
with higher Pass@1 and Pass⁴.

For GPT-6-sol, RiseHarness improves Pass@1 by 5.25% and 3.09% on TBH and
TB2.1, respectively, while increasing the all-success task fraction on
both benchmarks. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash, RiseHarness improves TBH Pass@1
by 7.25% and Pass⁴ by 14%. Pass@4 increases only modestly in comparison,
suggesting that the main gain is in repeated-run success reliability
rather than a large expansion in observed task coverage.

##### Performance across iterations.

Figures
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
show task outcome distributions and pass rates, respectively, as four
mechanisms for completion confirmation accumulate for DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
Each version retains the preceding changes and adds one mechanism; their
definitions and triggers appear in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Model-Specific Adaptation ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").
On TBH, despite fluctuations among intermediate versions, the final
version achieves the highest average pass rate and all-success task
fraction, while reducing both flipping and all-failure tasks relative to
the seed harness. These results show that changes to shared interaction
behaviors can yield improvements in performance and reliability when
combined and evaluated iteratively.

The gains also extend to TB2.1, which was not used for evolution.
Directly applying the final version selected on TBH improves Pass@1 by
3.09% and Pass⁴ by 6.74% over Terminus-2, showing that the benefits are
not confined to the tasks that produced the proposals. Version rankings
differ between benchmarks: the three-mechanism version achieves higher
observed performance on TB2.1, whereas the four-mechanism final version
performs best on TBH. Overall, the results show that RiseHarness
improves success and reliability on the evolution tasks and also
benefits the same model on a benchmark not used for evolution.

### 4.3 Component Contributions

We use two ablations to examine the contributions of harness execution
evidence and external design research to harness evolution for
DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Apart from the removed component, the analysis,
implementation, and evaluation procedures remain unchanged.

##### Execution evidence.

Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Performance across iterations. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
compares full RiseHarness with the variant without harness traces or the
Handbook. The ablated variant retains access to agent traces and source
code and follows the same external research procedure. On TBH, the full
method achieves Pass@1 and Pass⁴ gains of 7% and 8%, respectively,
indicating that harness traces and the Handbook provide useful
information beyond agent traces and source code. On TB2.1, the full
method also outperforms the ablated variant on both metrics, supporting
the joint contribution of these two sources of information to the
evolved harness.

##### External research.

Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Performance across iterations. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
compares full RiseHarness with the variant that generates proposals
using only local information. Both variants use dual traces and the
Handbook; they differ in whether they search for external designs and
implementations. On TBH, the full method improves Pass@1 and Pass⁴ by
5.50% and 6%, respectively, while achieving higher Pass@4 and lower
Flip. On TB2.1, the full method also maintains higher average success
and all-success task fractions. These results suggest that external
research usefully complements local execution analysis, with benefits on
both the evolution tasks and tasks not used for evolution.

### 4.4 Adaptation and Generalization

##### Model-specific behavioral requirements.

The retained changes differ across models. DeepSeek-V4-Flash strengthens
the evidence required for completion, whereas GPT-6-sol emphasizes
execution continuity and feedback through session recovery, workspace
diffs, and prior-work evidence. Figure
[4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
locates these changes; Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Model-Specific Adaptation ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
describes their mechanisms.

Figure 7: Model-adapted vs. swapped final harnesses ($`r=4`$). GPT:
GPT-6-sol; DeepSeek: DeepSeek-V4-Flash, using its final + IR harness.
Y-axes start above zero.

Figure
[7](#S4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Model-specific behavioral requirements. ‣ 4.4 Adaptation and Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
compares each model’s final harness with the harness evolved for the
other model. Both models perform better with their own harnesses on both
benchmarks (full results in Appendix
[D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Cross-Model Transfer ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")).

##### Cross-benchmark generalization.

We freeze the harnesses evolved on TBH and evaluate them on TB2.1 with
the execution model unchanged. Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Performance across iterations. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
compares performance with Terminus-2. Both models retain gains in
average success and all-success task fraction on TB2.1; the direct
transfer of DeepSeek’s final + IR version is reported in Appendix
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Evolution Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").
Together, the transfer experiments show that harness improvements can
extend to unseen tasks while remaining sensitive to the model executing
them.

## 5 Conclusion

We presented RiseHarness, a framework that iteratively improves the
harness to increase task success and execution reliability for
long-horizon terminal agents while keeping model weights fixed. Starting
from flipping tasks, it contrasts successful and failed runs under the
same configuration and combines agent trajectories, internal harness
traces, and a Harness Handbook to connect execution problems to specific
interaction behaviors and their implementations. It then searches other
harness frameworks for relevant designs and develops proposals suited to
the current execution flow, available signals, and model behavior.
Implementation checks and repeated evaluation determine whether a change
is retained. Accepted versions, together with their updated Handbooks
and execution evidence, become the basis for subsequent iterations.

Our experiments show that harness evolution can improve average task
performance and increase the fraction of tasks solved consistently
across repeated runs. Ablations further support the contributions of
harness execution evidence and external design research: the former
exposes internal processing that agent trajectories alone may not
reveal, while the latter provides design options beyond local analysis.
The changes retained for different models target different behaviors and
use different interventions. Swapping the evolved harnesses between
models reduces performance, supporting model-specific harness
adaptation. At the same time, frozen harnesses retain gains on a
benchmark not used for evolution, demonstrating the transfer value of
improvements to interaction mechanisms shared across tasks.

These findings show that systematic harness analysis and evolution can
help models use their existing capabilities more reliably, alongside
improvements to the models themselves. Future work will examine the
approach across more models, task distributions, and agent frameworks,
and explore ways to reduce the evaluation cost of harness evolution.

## Appendix A System Implementation

This appendix supplements Sections
[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Execution Evidence ‣ 3 Harness Self-Evolution ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")–[3.5](#S3.SS5 "3.5 Validation and Evolution ‣ 3 Harness Self-Evolution ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Agent harnesses. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").
Model-specific mechanisms, evaluation rules, and supplementary results
follow in Appendices
[B](#A2 "Appendix B Model-Specific Adaptation ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"),
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Evaluation Methodology ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"),
and
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"),
respectively. Worked examples for both models and saved prompt excerpts
appear in Sections
[A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Case Studies ‣ Appendix A System Implementation ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and
[A.5](#A1.SS5 "A.5 Prompt Examples ‣ Appendix A System Implementation ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

### A.1 Evidence and Versioning

Each reference corpus $`R_{t}`$ contains task outcomes and paired agent
and harness traces under the current harness $`H_{t}`$. Run identifiers
and episode indices connect model requests to the internal calls that
process them and the observations returned to the model. The monitor
records selected function boundaries, including arguments, returns,
exceptions, caller relationships, and source locations. The Handbook
$`K_{t}`$ maps these records to behavioral responsibilities and
implementing functions. The two sources are complementary: traces
describe observed execution, while the Handbook supplies the behavioral
structure used to interpret it.

A candidate comprises source changes, mechanism settings, an updated
Handbook, and a compatible recording configuration. Smoke checks
establish that it can run and record traces. On adoption, these
artifacts are saved together with the full evaluation outcomes and
traces $`E_{t}`$. They become the next harness, Handbook, and reference
corpus, keeping subsequent analysis tied to the accepted implementation.
Rejection preserves the current version.

### A.2 Behavioral Validation

When independent behavioral checking is enabled, each implemented
mechanism has a contract describing its trigger conditions, observable
effects, relevant hooks and state, and runtime setting. Dependencies,
replacements, and conflicts specify which mechanisms may be enabled
together. These checks concern the implementation of a proposed
behavior; task evaluation measures its effect on performance.

Contracts include positive and negative cases and recovery cases where
applicable. For an input $`x`$, let $`o^{-}(x)`$ denote the expected
incumbent behavior and $`o^{+}(x)`$ the expected modified behavior. An
independent observer first checks the incumbent expectation before the
contract is frozen. The implementation is then checked in three
configurations:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle O(H_{t},x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=o^{-}(x),`$ |  | (3) |
|  | $`\displaystyle O(C_{t},\text{new mechanisms disabled},x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=o^{-}(x),`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle O(C_{t},\text{mechanism and dependencies enabled},x)`$ | $`\displaystyle=o^{+}(x).`$ |  |  |

The disabled configuration checks preservation of incumbent behavior,
while the enabled configuration checks the intended intervention.
Observed results are compared with the frozen expectations; a process
crash cannot establish successful handling of a negative case. Failures
are returned for repair within the configured attempt limit. These
finite cases do not guarantee correctness on all tasks or isolate a
mechanism that executes with dependencies.

### A.3 Iteration Management

Each round links proposals, checks, outcomes, and execution evidence to
the candidate. The history $`\mathcal{L}`$ guides implementation repair,
proposal revision, alternative proposals, or renewed discovery after
adoption. The proposing model may differ from the fixed evaluated model
$`M_{\theta}`$.

The round limit $`T`$ and policy $`\Pi`$ bound this process. Candidates
must pass the configured checks before evaluation; adoption requires a
valid, complete full evaluation under the aggregate pass-rate rule in
Appendix
[C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Comparison Protocol ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Methodology ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").
Screening alone cannot promote a candidate.

group, external research, proposal, implementation report, and
evaluation receipts. The displayed fields are copied in full, without
rewriting their values; LaTeX escaping and line wrapping affect
presentation only. Other fields, including long repeated call indexes,
are omitted. File names and JSON pointers identify the excerpts.
Internal run numbers, join keys, and opaque task identifiers are omitted
from the reading copy. The underlying complete records and their SHA-256
hashes are retained with the source package. These are the pipeline’s
contemporaneous outputs, including its hypotheses and limitations,
rather than retrospective explanations of why a task failed.
Source-local behavior codes and function names are preserved inside
quotations.

## Appendix B Model-Specific Adaptation

This appendix describes the changes analyzed in Section
[4.4](#S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1 "Model-specific behavioral requirements. ‣ 4.4 Adaptation and Generalization ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"),
separating what each mechanism does from its measured effects. The two
main models are presented first; the earlier GPT-5.6-Terra change is
included separately. Evaluation rules and numerical results follow in
Appendices
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Evaluation Methodology ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

### B.1 GPT-6-sol

The three retained changes improve execution continuity and the evidence
returned to the model. Their behavioral locations follow the seed
Handbook: session liveness is checked by the Interaction main loop;
persisted changes are presented during Observation construction and
output truncation; and completion-specific context is supplied during
the Completion confirmation handshake.

##### Completion-claim context.

When the agent declares completion, the confirmation message includes
evidence of the work performed earlier in the run, rather than only an
idle terminal prompt. This modification targets the Completion
confirmation handshake, supported by observation construction and the
recorded execution history. Its implementation setting is
completion_claim_context.

##### Persisted workspace feedback.

The harness presents changes actually written to files as a workspace
diff. The feedback is grounded in persisted file contents rather than
terminal echo, giving the agent a view of what changed. Its primary
behavioral location is Observation construction and output truncation,
with file inspection supplying the underlying evidence. Its setting is
persisted_workspace_diff.

##### Session-loss recovery.

When the terminal session disappears, the harness recovers the session
and informs the agent of the resulting state loss. This changes the
Interaction main loop’s handling of session liveness, with tmux session
operations and observation construction supporting recovery and its
feedback. Its setting is single_session_loss_recovery.

### B.2 DeepSeek-V4-Flash

In the seed harness, the first completion declaration requests
confirmation, and a second consecutive declaration permits termination.
The four adopted modifications add checks to this handshake. In Figures
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents"),
SE denotes structured evidence, DI designated invocation, OO observed
operand, and IR independent reading. The corresponding behaviors are
detailed below. Each check can withhold completion at most once per run,
providing a bounded opportunity for correction rather than enforcing an
indefinitely repeated verification requirement.

##### Primary and supporting stages.

The primary stage is where a modification changes a harness decision or
action; supporting stages acquire its inputs or maintain the required
state. For example, designated-invocation verification reads command
history recorded during dispatch but changes the completion decision
during the handshake. All four modifications therefore target Completion
confirmation handshake, with their supporting stages listed in Table
[2](#A2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Primary and supporting stages. ‣ B.2 DeepSeek-V4-Flash ‣ Appendix B Model-Specific Adaptation ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

|  Behavior |  Primary stage |  Supporting stages |
|----|----|----|
|  Executable completion verification (SE) |  Completion confirmation handshake |  LLM query and context rescue; Response parsing and command extraction: preserve and parse the verification command and expected exit code. |
|  Designated-invocation verification (DI) |  Completion confirmation handshake |  Command dispatch and timeout handling: record dispatched commands. |
|  Completion-outcome observation (OO) |  Completion confirmation handshake |  LLM query and context rescue; Response parsing and command extraction: obtain verification fields for the environment probe. |
|  Independent-reading corroboration (IR) |  Completion confirmation handshake |  Command dispatch and timeout handling; Observation construction and output truncation: record commands and construct observations containing reading results. |

Table 2: Behavioral modifications for DeepSeek-V4-Flash and their
Handbook mappings.

##### Executable completion verification (SE).

The model supplies a verification command and its expected exit code in
the completion declaration. The harness executes the command and
compares its exit code with the expected value. A match permits this
check to release completion; missing fields, execution failure, or a
mismatch produce one request to continue working. This makes the model’s
completion evidence executable by the harness, while preserving the
bounded withholding rule.

##### Designated-invocation verification (DI).

When a task explicitly specifies an invocation, the harness checks
whether it appears in the dispatched-command history. It conservatively
extracts the interpreter, script, and arguments from the task
instruction, and accommodates absolute paths and relative script paths
after a directory change through basename matching. The check triggers
only when an alternative invocation has been observed but the designated
invocation has not. It then requests that the model execute the
specified invocation before confirming completion again.

##### Completion-outcome observation (OO).

On the second completion declaration, the harness executes the supplied
verification command through the session’s environment interface, with a
30-second probe limit. The check compares an observed integer exit code
with the expected value and records a successful match as well as a
withholding decision. Missing evidence, a non-integer result, or a
mismatch can withhold completion once. If the sandbox call raises an
exception, this check fails open, so the probe exception does not itself
turn into a task failure.

##### Independent-reading corroboration (IR).

This check uses existing execution history rather than launching another
command. It relates dispatched commands, normalized reading-method
signatures, input objects, and values extracted from subsequent
observations. If a reading used to support completion is backed by only
one method, the harness requests a different form of inspection or a
second independent reading method. Repeating the same method is not
treated as independent corroboration.

##### Implementation boundaries.

Executable completion verification and completion-outcome observation
are separate checks and can execute the same verification command twice.
Their effects are therefore overlapping. Independent-reading
corroboration primarily detects reliance on a single reading method: the
current evidence-set construction makes the separate
conflicting-readings branch largely unreachable. We consequently do not
describe it as a general consistency checker. These are implementation
boundaries, not estimates of the individual mechanisms’ causal
contributions. The full cumulative measurements and their evaluation
provenance are reported in Appendix
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Evolution Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

### B.3 GPT-5.6-Terra

The earlier GPT-5.6-Terra modification targets Command dispatch and
timeout handling. A command can contain a literal tab as input data; if
tmux interprets it as a special key event, the terminal receives
different input from the model’s intended command. Literal
control-character transport preserves the character as data during
dispatch. This changes command transport rather than completion
confirmation. Its results are reported separately in Appendix
[D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 GPT-5.6-Terra ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and do not establish the changes needed by GPT-6-sol.

## Appendix C Evaluation Methodology

This appendix supplements Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1 "Models and benchmarks. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
with scoring, baseline, and version-reporting rules. Numerical results
follow in Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents").

### C.1 Repeated Evaluation

The default $`r=4`$ gives 400 trial slots for TBH and 356 for TB2.1. The
metrics in Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3 "Metrics and reporting. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
require a complete grid. Passes score $`1`$; task failures and completed
runtime failures with valid records score $`0`$, retaining their
harness, infrastructure, or unknown-error classification. Missing,
cancelled, or identity-mismatched measurements are $`\bot`$ and cannot
be dropped to make an incomplete grid valid. Blank table entries mean
unreported results, not failures.

Aggregate outcome proportions do not identify which initially stable
tasks regressed; paired per-task outcomes are needed.

### C.2 Comparison Protocol

Before evaluating a candidate, the policy specifies the comparison
baseline. For stage $`s`$ on task set $`S`$, it selects either
historical reference runs or a newly measured incumbent control:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\widehat{p}_{B}^{\,s}(S)=\begin{cases}\widehat{p}(R_{t}|_{S}),&b_{s}=\mathrm{historical},\\
\widehat{p}(H_{t};S,r_{s}),&b_{s}=\mathrm{fresh}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (4) |

Here $`r_{s}`$ is the stage’s repetition count. Historical comparisons
use their stored repetitions and corresponding denominator. The
controller defaults to historical reuse; fresh controls are optional.
Historical source identity does not establish unchanged service or
environment conditions, so baseline provenance remains part of the
evaluation record.

Adoption requires a valid, complete full evaluation with aggregate pass
rate above the declared baseline. Previously stable tasks may regress
despite an overall gain, so reliability is reported separately from the
adoption score.

### C.3 Result Reporting

The main comparison, cumulative curves, and transfer experiment refer to
explicitly identified harness versions. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, TBH uses
the final four-mechanism version (+ IR). Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Overall performance. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
and Figure
[6](#S4.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Performance across iterations. ‣ 4.2 Performance and Reliability ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
report the best observed TB2.1 three-mechanism version (+ OO), selected
by its TB2.1 score. This is distinct from directly transferring the
final version selected on TBH. The full sequence in Appendix
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Evolution Results ‣ Appendix D Supplementary Results ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
keeps both versions visible. TB2.1 does not inform harness
modifications; selection by its observed score is nevertheless part of
this reporting protocol.

The four non-base TBH versions use the original $`100\times 4`$ grid.
The seed’s TBH result is 227/400 passes (56.75%), with 37 all-success,
34 flipping, and 29 all-failure tasks. For the first three non-base
TB2.1 versions, controller-timeout slots were rerun and merged with the
other results; the final version uses a complete rerun. These
differences in evaluation assembly are retained when interpreting the
cumulative sequence. The curves measure combined harness versions rather
than isolated causal effects of individual mechanisms.

## Appendix E Scope and Limitations

##### Execution evidence and analysis coverage.

Successful runs provide references for failure analysis, but differences
may also reflect sampling, environment variation, or task difficulty.
Discovery from traceable flipping tasks excludes consistently failing
tasks and failures before recording. The monitor covers selected
boundaries, and the Handbook may omit behavior or become stale. Neither
source establishes causality.

##### Candidate changes and regression risks.

External designs may require unavailable interfaces or signals.
Behavioral checks cover finite cases, while combined-candidate
evaluation does not isolate individual mechanisms. Aggregate-score
adoption can retain changes that harm previously stable tasks; aggregate
outcome proportions cannot quantify these regressions without per-task
comparisons.

##### Evaluation and transfer.

Repeated development-set selection can exploit noise, and historical
baselines are sensitive to service or environment drift. Retained-score
trends therefore require independent evaluation. The reporting protocol
in Appendix
[C.3](#A3.SS3 "C.3 Result Reporting ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Methodology ‣ Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents")
distinguishes target-selected versions from frozen final-version
transfer. Cross-model swapping shows model dependence for the tested
harnesses, without ruling out transfer of individual mechanisms between
other models.

##### Scope and resource costs.

Other harnesses require compatible monitoring, behavioral mappings, and
evaluation adapters. Long runs, external research, and repeated
evaluation incur inference and storage costs; configured concurrency is
not measured speedup. LLMCarbon motivates broader resource accounting
\[[39](#bib.bib39)\], but emissions are not measured here. The loop
keeps model weights fixed and does not learn its outer controller.
Training-side methods, including work on asynchronous policy mismatch
\[[40](#bib.bib40)\], are complementary directions for future study.
````
